Here is a small trick that makes your English sound more polite. Compare two questions. Are you using the meeting room this afternoon? And: will you be using the meeting room this afternoon? The second one is softer. Why? Because it asks about your plan, not about a decision. It does not sound like I want something from you. It just sounds like I am organizing the day. That is why receptionists, flight attendants and good colleagues use it all the time. Will you be joining us for dinner? Will you be needing a taxi tomorrow? So next time you ask about someone's schedule, try this form. It is a small change, and people will hear the difference.

Hi Vanessa, it's Marcos from the Porto Alegre office. I'm calling about our call next week. I'm afraid I'll be running a workshop all day on Thursday, so I can't do Thursday morning. Could we bring it forward to Wednesday? I'll be working from home that day, so any time after nine is fine for me. If Wednesday doesn't work for you, I have a free slot on Friday at eleven, but that one is tentative, because I might be visiting a client. Let's touch base by email tomorrow and pencil something in. Thanks, Vanessa, and talk soon.

First, I check my calendar for the next few days. Then I ask politely: will you be working from the office on Wednesday? After that, I offer two free slots and we pencil one in. Next, if something changes, I bring the meeting forward or move it. In the end, we touch base the day before to confirm.
